zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check after scan reading: NINJAL, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510; developed by Hideyuki Ohshima with assistance from Taichi Aida, CC BY 4.0 (https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html). The index is an aid, not the authority for this copy's typography or wording.

lines.note: Mancai is glossed as thousands of worlds. The initial M is worn but the sequence ncai is recoverable; the complete short definition belongs to one flush-left entry row.
Mandara names a Buddhist picture or representation. The damaged internal n retains its upper arch, correcting Maudara; Bup. is upright, including its period. No hyphen is visible after the final al.
Gũa completes algũa across the preceding line break. The tilde remains over u in this fragment, and the phrase completes the description of a portrait or picture.

runs.text: Dez mil lanternas, ou candeas que

lines.note: Mandô denotes the ten thousand lamps or lights used in a religious setting. The headword has a visible circumflex; preserve candeas without modernizing it to candeias.

runs.text: ſe acendem às vezes diante do Fotoque.

lines.note: The lights are sometimes lit before the Fotoque. Fotoque is a Japanese religious term embedded in the Portuguese sentence, and the printed às retains its grave accent.
Mandocoro is explained as an official such as an overseer of finances. Official and veador are historical spellings; the clear fazen- break continues on the next row.
Da completes fazenda, followed by the alternative office of governor. This short italic row is an indented continuation, not a separate entry.
Mandocu is paraphrased as Yorozzuno tocu, all virtues or attributes. The Portuguese atri- continues below; the Japanese paraphrase is not an embedded Portuguese font-toggle term.

runs.text: butos, & virtudes, ou todos os bẽs. ¶

lines.note: Butos completes atributos, and the definition includes all goods or virtues. The example begins Von, with a pointed capital V rather than Y; enlargement shows no terminal hyphen before the rule.

runs.text: aruji Deusni xojen mandocu ſonauari ta-

lines.note: The Japanese sentence attributes all goodness and virtue to Deus. Its roman text continues both from the previous row and into ta-mǒ below; retain the printed spelling and division.

runs.text: Em Deos hà todos os bẽs, & virtudes.

lines.note: Mǒ completes the Japanese honorific verb. The Portuguese says that all goods and virtues are in God; the scan reads todos, not OCR indos, and retains the abbreviated bẽs.
Mandoqi refers to the hours around midday. The historical Portuguese meo dia is printed as two words and is not modernized.
Mane, uru, eta is the historical verb for mimicking or imitating. The displayed paradigm licenses the manuru form in the following example; Vt is italic with the gloss.
Fitouo manuru is the standalone example of imitating someone. Its short roman row remains indented and is not treated as Portuguese-embedded Japanese for font toggling.
The noun Mane denotes imitation. The pilcrow introduces Fitono maneuo, continued by ſuru below; the entry and example remain on their actual physical rows.
The printed ſuru completes Fitono maneuo from the preceding row. The Portuguese gives the sense of imitating someone and retains unaccented alguem.
Maneqi, u, eita means beckoning with the hands. The historical verb and its past ending are legible; the gloss uses capear rather than a modern replacement.
Fitouo maneqiyoſuru describes calling someone over. The gloss begins Chamar a al- and continues below; the long ſ in the Japanese compound is retained.

runs.text: guem com acenos das mãos. Per met.

lines.note: Guem completes alguem, and the action is explained as hand gestures. Per met. introduces a metaphorical extension beginning with Bat, the Japanese term continued in the next row.
Bat uo manequ means inviting punishment; the Portuguese gives justice and punishment. Preserve Grangear and the provisional printed st classifications in justiça and caſtigo.
Vazauaiuo manequ means bringing misfortune upon oneself. The Portuguese verb visibly has two r letters in Acarretar, correcting the single-r OCR, and the gloss continues below.
The Portuguese continuation specifies troubles and losses. The long ſ in ocaſionar and the final &c. are preserved; no additional Japanese example begins on this row.
The compound means gathering people by beckoning. Enlargement reads acenã- with a nasal abbreviation and a terminal hyphen, correcting the garbled OCR; do completes the participle below.
Do completes the preceding Portuguese participle before the alternative capeando. Fǒbaidomouo ma- begins an example about gathering companions, with a real hyphen after ma.
Neqi atçumuru completes the gathering expression. The Portuguese translates it as assembling companions; the Japanese cedilla and the physical split of maneqi are retained.

runs.text: ainda que ſeja ſem lhes capear.

lines.note: The definition extends to gathering companions even without literally beckoning to them. The row is wholly Portuguese italic and ends the previous entry.

Mangamare describes something exceedingly rare. The example visibly abbreviates the first nasal as Mãga, with a mark above a; no hyphen is printed at this row end. Retain the ß-shaped sort in rarißima.
The Japanese example concerns a rare visit. The Portuguese begins A voſſa vinda, not the OCR pilcrow and coſſa; both separate long-ſ letters are visible in voſſa.
The Portuguese completes the statement that the visit is very rare. Retain the historical he and mui rather than replacing them with modern forms.

runs.text: Pãſinhos de trigo cozidos com o ba-

lines.note: Mangiǔ names steamed wheat buns. The final u has a caron, not OCR b. Enlargement reads the historical diminutive Pãſinhos with long ſ; do not modernize it to pãezinhos.
Fo completes bafo: the buns are cooked with the vapor of hot water. Preserve the historical joined dagoa and the physical ba-fo division.

runs.text: Caſa onde fazem, ou vendem eſ-

lines.note: Mangiǔya is the place where these buns are made or sold. The final u has the same caron as the preceding headword; Caſa onde and vendem repair clear OCR errors in the gloss.
Tes completes eſtes, referring back to the buns in the preceding entry. The printed plural is pãis, not modern pães, and its nasal mark is retained.
Manguat is paraphrased by Tçuqi mitçuru, the moon becoming full. The gloss Lũa chea and both Japanese cedillas are preserved as printed.

The example compares something to a full moon rising over mountains. Retain the aligned Maguatno: a faint trace above its first a might be a nasal mark, but it is too weak and close to the preceding descender to supply confidently.

runs.text: ſi como a lũa chea aponta por cima dos mõtes.

lines.note: This completes Aſ-ſi and the comparison with a full moon rising above the mountains. The last abbreviated word is mõtes, with a round o under the tilde, correcting OCR mãtes.
Manguei denotes all arts or skills and is paraphrased as Yorozzuno guei. This complete one-row entry requires no change to the historical Japanese spelling.
Manguet is identified with Manguat, another full-moon form. The small mark after i is a comma, and the Japanese synonym is not a Portuguese-embedded typeface term.
Manguiǒ denotes all virtuous practices, as the Japanese paraphrase and continuation explain. The headword ends in a marked o, not the OCR long ſ; retain the printed iǒ sequence.
Obras virtuoſas completes the all-practices definition. This short Portuguese row is indented and ends with a visible period.

Mani ai first denotes torinoco paper for folding screens. The gloss reads Papel torinoco pera Biǒbus, with a downward-pointing mark over o; torinoco and Biǒbus are Japanese terms within Portuguese. The printed Item ends with a comma.

runs.text: Esteira do tamanho & largura de hum Tatami.

lines.note: The second sense is a mat of the size and width of a tatami. The initial word is Esteira, correcting Eildra; its st class is left in the normal provisional spelling.
Maniaino muxiro illustrates the mat sense, followed by italic Idem. The example is standalone Japanese, so its individual words are not font-toggle targets.
The entry denotes overflowing. A visible word-sized gap separates Man and it; the paraphrase is Michi afururu, not Michai. The gloss reads Treſbordar with an ascending b, not the OCR p.
The continuation adds being very full to the overflowing sense. Preserve the provisional long-ſt form eſtar and the historical cheo.
Manjen is paraphrased as Yorozzuno jen and glossed as many or all virtues. The damaged headword and gloss are recoverable from their letterforms; jen has a descending j, not OCR ien.
As virtudes completes the Manjen gloss. The scan clearly has as rather than OCR ai, and this is the last body row of the left column.
This Manji means reaching the completion or full measure of something. The Portuguese prints Comprirſe, a historical form retained without modernization, and al- carries into the next row.
Gum completes algum, and the gloss specifies a period of time or age. Ficazuga mã- begins the example about a completed number of days; the nasal abbreviation is printed above a.
Jita completes mã-jita, followed by the translation that the number of days was fulfilled. Restore the continuation indentation visible in the scan; the row is not a new entry.
A second Manji entry concerns becoming proud. Its paradigm is separately printed, and the pilcrow begins Vareto, continued in the next row.
Miuo manjezare completes a warning against becoming proud. The historical negative imperative is retained, as is the Portuguese cedilla in enſoberbeçais.
Manjin is explained by Manqina fito, a proud person. The final S. is the dictionary’s written-usage label, not part of the Japanese synonym, and its locally aligned typography is retained.
Manju is paraphrased as Mitçuru tama, a filling jewel. The gloss introduces a precious stone whose reputed effect is specified in the following rows.

runs.text: precioſa que ſegundo as fabulas dos gentios

lines.note: The precious stone is described according to what the dictionary calls the gentiles’ fables. This reports the source’s attribution rather than asserting the supernatural property as fact.
The source attributes the rising tide to the jewel. Enlargement shows an acute stroke over the final e in maré, not the OCR tilde; retain the claim as part of the historical definition.
Manjuxaqe names a red flower, termed roſa by the Portuguese gloss. The definition continues with its autumn flowering; no modern botanical identification is inserted.
Florece no Outono completes the seasonal description of the red flower. Preserve the historical florece spelling and the capital O of Outono.
Manmacu denotes curtains used in an army or other settings. The long ſ in ſeruem is clear, and exercito remains unaccented as in the scan.
The continuation adds use aboard a vessel or at home. Preserve the singular embarcação and the historical caſa spelling; the row closes the curtain definition.
Man man is spaced as two components and paraphrased by Mitçuru. Its meaning is filling or being full, with estar retaining the baseline st classification.
The separate Manman entry means thousands upon thousands. Its example starts Man- at the rule, with a visible break before mantaru on the next row.
Mantaru caixǒni funauatari ſu describes navigating an immense sea. The marked o in caixǒni is visible; S. is a usage label before the Portuguese Naue- continuation.
Gar completes Nauegar. The translation describes sailing on immense seas; retain the tightly joined pormares and the double m in immenſos.
Mannaca denotes a half or the middle. The Portuguese alternative meyo is the historical spelling actually printed, not modern meio.
Mannô is paraphrased as Yorozzuno nô, all arts or abilities. Both o vowels have upward-pointing circumflexes; the following row provides a proverb-like expression.
Mannô ixxin introduces an explanation contrasting many skills with a person’s character. This standalone Japanese phrase is not an embedded Portuguese typeface target.

runs.text: boas em hũ homẽ, ſe elle he ruim, ou tem ruins

lines.note: The explanation allows a person to possess many good arts while still being bad or badly behaved. Hũ and homẽ retain their printed nasal abbreviations rather than being expanded.
The sentence concludes that bad habits make those talents of no use. The whole indented row is Portuguese, and the negative não remains as printed.
Manqei denotes all fine prospects or views. Xenqei begins the Japanese example continued below; preserve the provisional ſt classification in the Portuguese viſtas.
Manqei completes Xenqei manqei, with italic Idem referring back to the stated meaning. The short Japanese continuation remains part of the example, not a new headword.
Manqi means pride. The pilcrow introduces Manqiuo vocoſu, raising or developing pride; the long ſ is retained in the Japanese verb.
The first phrase translates the preceding example as becoming proud. A second example, Mãqini focoru, retains its visible nasal abbreviation, and A- begins the Portuguese verb on the next row.
Leuantarſe completes A-leuantarſe and describes rising with pride. Retain the historical verb form and long ſ, not a modernized formulation.
Manqijin and Manqinamono are alternative names for a proud person. The connector l is the printed alternative marker; neither Japanese synonym is a Portuguese-embedded term.

runs.text: Todos os Bonzos q̃ ha nalgũa tera &

lines.note: Manſan covers all the monks belonging to a tera and its precincts. Tera is a Japanese temple term embedded in the Portuguese definition; retain the abbreviated q̃ and nalgũa.

runs.text: dentro da cerca em varias ermidas, ou cellas.

lines.note: The definition includes monks in separate hermitages or cells within the enclosure. Varias and cellas retain the printed spelling and lack of modern accentuation.
Manſanno xuye illustrates an assembly belonging to the temple community. The gloss begins Ajuntamento de and continues with the assembled monks below; Vt remains italic.
The translation completes an assembly of all monks of a particular Tera. Tera is a Japanese temple word within the Portuguese sentence and is a font-toggle target.
Manſui means being full of water. The pilcrow starts Manſuino, which modifies iqe on the next row; preserve the long ſ and historical agoa.
Iqe completes the Japanese example of a full pond. Tanque is Portuguese but is visibly upright in this line, unlike the italic continuation; its unusual local typography is preserved.
Mantenno yuqi describes densely falling snow. The gloss retains Neue, cae and the provisional st classification in basta, rather than imposing modern spellings.

runs.text: com que fica o ar cheo, & como coalhado.

lines.note: The continuation says that the air becomes full and, as it were, curdled with snow. Coalhado is the source’s comparison and is retained literally.
Manucare, ruru, eta means escaping danger. The historical conjugation is printed with ruru; no modernized manukareru form is substituted.
The Japanese example says that human beings cannot escape birth and death. Preserve xǒjiuo and the separated yezu; the final italic O begins the Portuguese translation.

runs.text: homem não pode eſcapar de nacer, & mor-

lines.note: The translation continues the impossibility of escaping birth and death. Retain nacer, the long ſ in eſcapar, and the aligned mor- break at the right edge.
Rer completes morrer, followed by the written-usage label S. This short indented continuation is not separate furniture or a new entry.
Manxin is paraphrased as Manqina cocoro, a proud heart. The Portuguese so-berbo breaks across rows; the crop was expanded upward to include the full initial M.
Berbo completes ſoberbo, the proud-heart gloss. The entire short row is Portuguese italic, indented beneath its headword.
Manza is paraphrased as Zani mitçuru and describes rooms being full. The long ſ in ſalas and the provisional ſt form in Eſtarem remain as printed.
Zaxiquis completes the Portuguese description of full rooms and visibly begins with capital Z. Cunxi manza ſureba then starts a standalone Japanese maxim, continued below.
This completes the maxim contrasting cultivated and lesser people. Enlargement shows a circumflex in xôjin, not the OCR caron; the Portuguese Zaxiqui is an embedded Japanese room term.

runs.text: varões ſabios, não tem lugar a gẽte baixa, &

lines.note: The translation says that a room full of wise men leaves no place for lowly people. The native line separates the article a from gẽte; preserve that space and the nasal abbreviation.

Ordinaria completes the contrast with ordinary people. The new phrase is Manzano xǔ, with a marked u rather than OCR xn; its Portuguese gloss continues on the next page, anticipated by the separate catchword.
